newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: AILING HAVEL SEEKS NEW TERM AS CZECH PRESIDENT.
newsitem.headline: AILING HAVEL SEEKS NEW TERM AS CZECH PRESIDENT.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel ended months of speculation about his future plans on Saturday by announcing that he would seek another term of office when his current mandate ends next February.

Speaking at a garden news conference at Prague Castle, the 60-year-old Havel, a former dissident playwright who led Prague's bloodless 1989 overthrow of the Communist government said that the four leading parties had asked him to stand again, despite serious health problems earlier this year.

"It was a difficult decision to take, but what prevailed eventually was my feeling of responsibility for general affairs and the service for my fellow citizens, and a feeling that I am willing to place service for (society) before my own comfort," Havel said.

There had been some speculation that Havel would forego his candidacy for the post -- which is elected by parliament -- after he nearly died following surgery to remove a small malignant tumour from his lungs last December.

Although he suffered through a harrowing recovery, Havel has since returned to full duties as president. There have been no reports of the cancer recurring, but doctors convinced him to give up his several-pack-a-day cigarette habit.
His difficult recovery and his unexpected marriage soon after leaving hospital to a Czech actress, had people questioning how Havel wants to spend the rest of his life.
Despite coughing frequently during the news conference, Havel sounded like he was determined to fight on.
"I would like to place quality before quantity and make fewer speeches in favour of more important speeches," Havel said, with his new wife Dagmar looking on.
No other candidates have yet to emerge to challenge Havel, who remains broadly popular and many Czechs have difficulty seeing somebody taking his place.
"I can't imagine who else could be the candidate?" Michael Zantovsky, chairman of one of the parties in the ruling coalition said in the daily Mlada Fronta Dnes on Saturday.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus issued a statement immediately after the announcement on Saturday saying his Civic Democratic Party fully backed Havel for a new term.

Havel's current five-year term began soon after the split of Czechoslovakia into two independent states in 1993. His only challenger at that time was a candidate of the ultra-right wing Republican party who received only a handful of votes.
Havel also served as the last Czechoslovak president from 1990 until just before the split.
This past week, he won his most sought-after foreign policy victory, when NATO invited the Czech Republic to become a full member of the alliance in 1999.

In an interview with Reuters before the invitation was issued, he said it would be "nice" if he would be the one to sign the final accession treaty for his country to enter NATO, after announcing the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact at the final meeting of the Soviet-led alliance in 1991.
"I would like to spend more time on internal (domestic) policy than I could in my previous term," Havel told the news conference on Saturday.

Days after he was released from hospital in January, he shocked the country by marrying a well-known stage and screen actress, Dagmar Veskrnova, now 44, who then took the Czech feminine name of Havlova.

Opinion polls show the president, who acts more as a philosophical balancing wheel for the country and is not affiliated with a political party, has maintained the solid popularity which brought him to power after the revolution.

There was however some negative reaction in the local press to his unexpected marriage. Havel bristles at these reports: "It is me, not other people, who will live with my wife," he told Reuters last week.

He frequently seems still like a dissident when he battles for the soul of Czech reforms with his long-time right-wing economist prime minister, Vaclav Klaus -- Havel preaching his gospel of the civic society, while Klaus espouses individualism.
